**No solution is correct.** Writing each composition's root as $-\Phi$ with $\alpha_4=a/4$, $\alpha_6=b/6$, $\alpha_9=c/9$, the set of distinct roots satisfies $V_n=\bigcup_s f_s(V_{n-1})$, where $f_s(v)=v/s+\alpha_s$ and $V_1=\{\alpha_4,\alpha_6,\alpha_9\}$. Then $R=|V_{20}|$.

**Solution 1 (21) is impossible.** Since $f_s$ is injective, $|V_n|\ge|V_{n-1}|$. If $|V_{n-1}|=m\ge 2$ and $|V_n|=m$, then all three images equal $V_n$, so $f_4,f_6,f_9$ agree at both the minimum and maximum of $V_{n-1}$. Two distinct affine maps with different slopes cannot agree at two points, so $|V_n|\ge|V_{n-1}|+1$. Then:
- If $|V_1|=2$, a case check over which two of $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ coincide shows $|V_2|=3$ is impossible, so $|V_2|\ge4$ and $R\ge 22$.
- If $|V_1|=3$, then $R\ge 22$.
- If $\alpha=\beta=\gamma\ne0$, then $|V_3|=9$, so $R\ge 26$.

So $R=21$ cannot occur for $R>1$.

**Solution 2 ($3^{19}$) is not the second smallest.** Take $a=3,\ b=5,\ c=8$. Then $f,g,h$ all share the fixed point $-1$, and every composition has root $-(1-P)$, where $P=2^{-X}3^{-(40-X)}$ with $X=2\#f+\#g\in[0,40]$. This gives exactly $41$ distinct roots, and $41<3^{19}$.

**Solution 3 ($(3^{20}+1)/2$)** is likewise far above the value $41$ already achieved, so it cannot be the second smallest.

The second smallest value is therefore at least 22 and at most 41, and none of the three proposed answers matches.
